sentences.text: Elections were held in the United States on November 3, 2026, during the second term of President Donald Trump, a Republican .
All 435 seats in the U.S. House of Representatives and 35 of the 100 seats in the U.S. Senate were contested to determine the 120th United States Congress.
Thirty-nine state and territorial U.S. gubernatorial elections, attorney general elections, and numerous state and local elections were also contested.
The Democratic Party won a majority of seats in both houses of Congress, and won numerous other offices currently held by Republicans.

Trump called on Republican-led states to enact rare mid-decade redistricting to boost the party's chances of holding power ahead of expected historical losses for the incumbent party during midterm elections, which prompted reciprocal redistricting.
In April 2026, the Supreme Court, in Louisiana v. Callais, narrowed the circumstances that Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act of 1965 applied to racial vote dilution.
The Trump administration used millions of taxpayer dollars to fund pro-administration advertisements, though it later switched to using money from President Trump's Super PAC.
Trump and Republicans made false claims of widespread voter fraud leading up to the elections, but ultimately accepted the results.

The lead-up to the elections was marked by an inflation surge amidst affordability concerns, particularly on gas, healthcare, and food prices, exacerbated by the Trump administration's tariffs and Strait of Hormuz crisis caused by the 2026 Iran War.

The growth of artificial intelligence became an unexpected issue, with voters concerned about AI-induced mass unemployment, its environmental impacts, mass surveillance, and the risk of human extinction from a hypothetically developed superintelligence.
Income inequality, democratic backsliding, corruption, and foreign policy were frequently cited among voters in scientific exit polling.
Trump made threats of annexing multiple countries and used executive orders to change the names of Lake Ontario ("Lake America") and the Gulf of Mexico ("Gulf of America").
The results were labeled a rebuke of President Trump, Trumpism, and further AI development.

It was "a fundamental realignment" in American politics, as Democrats won the largest popular-vote victory in the House of Representatives since 1976 in a lopsided electoral rout dubbed a "Blue Tsunami".

Democrats won Republican Senate seats in Iowa, Ohio, South Carolina, Maine, Kansas, North Carolina, and Texas, the last two by double digits; seats in Alaska and Mississippi remain uncalled by major media outlets as of November 5, with Democrats favored to win both elections.
They also flipped at least five governorships, granting them a majority of governorships for the first time since 2010.
In the 2024 United States presidential election, Republican nominee Donald Trump defeated Democratic nominee Kamala Harris.
Key issues shaping the campaign included public concern for the post-pandemic recovery and rising inflation.
ABC News, CBS News, Fox News, NBC News, the Associated Press, MS Now and CNN used the Voter Poll by SSRS to gather voter preferences and opinions for the 2026 elections.
From 2018 to 2024, ABC, NBC, CBS and CNN used data from the National Election Pool while the Associated Press and Fox News relied on AP VoteCast.
The Republican Party performed worse than expected in the November 2025 general elections.
Democratic candidates Abigail Spanberger of Virginia and Mikie Sherrill of New Jersey won their gubernatorial races over their Republican opponents by larger than expected margins.
Democrats performed strongly in the concurrent state legislative elections, winning a supermajority in the New Jersey General Assembly and expanding their majority in the Virginia House of Delegates.

In New York City, Democrat Zohran Mamdani, a self-identified democratic socialist, was elected mayor in a three-way race against Republican Curtis Sliwa and independent former governor Andrew Cuomo, who ran as a moderate relative to Mamdani.
The main theme of the elections was the United States affordability crisis.
According to the AP Voter Poll, about four in ten voters said they had voted to express opposition to Trump, compared with fewer than two in ten who said they had voted to express support for him.
Roughly four in ten said Trump was not a factor in their voting decision.
Voters' views of Trump's presidency were an important factor in the election.
During the 2025 off-year elections, exit polls found that many voted in opposition to Trump or said that he was not a factor.
Surveys released in late 2025 and early 2026 found that many viewed Trump's handling of the economy and immigration, two issues that propelled him to victory in the 2024 election, negatively.
During elections held in his first term, Trump was on the minds of many who voted.

In September 2026, Trump featured in a two-day midterm convention in Dallas to rally support and raise funds—historically, this type of event is reserved for presidential election years, although the Democratic National Committee had previously held midterm-year party conferences in 1974, 1978, and 1982.
Many Republicans on the ballot attended, but many also chose to forego the event, which RNC Chairman Joe Gruters dubbed a "Trump-a-Palooza".
The outbreak of the 2026 Iran war on February 28 introduced further complications, with rising gasoline prices and other economic challenges emerging as central electoral concerns.

Analysts argued that gasoline prices represented the most direct channel through which the costs of the Iran war were transmitted to American voters, and that domestic electoral pressure from fuel costs was a primary political driver behind the Trump administration's push toward a ceasefire ahead of the November midterms.
Polling released by CNN in the September 2026 showed that only 26% of voters approved of the Trump administration's handling of Iran.

In response to the general unpopularity and economic concerns of the Iran war, several Republican candidates have distanced themselves from Trump and his approach to the war and have called for operations in Iran to end.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer compared the political environment in 2026 to the one in 2006, when dissatisfaction with George W. Bush's handling of the Iraq War led to many Democratic victories in the elections that year.
Democratic candidates have leveraged the unpopularity of the war as a campaign point.
The nearly seven-month-old war in Iran became a political liability for some Republican candidates ahead of the November midterms.
In September 2026, two Republicans in tight Senate races—Mike Rogers of Michigan and Ashley Hinson of Iowa—called for a swift end to the conflict, distancing themselves from President Trump.
Hinson, who had voted six times against measures to curb Trump's war powers, said Iowans "shouldn't have to foot the bill at the pump or the checkout line for the war in Iran."
Rogers, who had previously backed Trump's strikes, released a campaign ad urging that the war "end and end quickly."
The shift came as Trump's approval rating fell to 32%, a career low, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll, with Americans souring on both his handling of the economy and the war.
Diesel prices reached record highs, a particular concern in Iowa, where agriculture plays an outsized role in the state's economy.

Other Republicans also moved to distance themselves: Iowa Representatives Zach Nunn and Mariannette Miller-Meeks reversed their stances and voted to limit Trump's war powers, while Representative Maria Elvira Salazar of Florida warned that Trump's immigration crackdown had gone too far.
Democrats characterized the moves as election-year repositioning.
By mid-October, the same polling series put Trump's approval at 31%—a record low for either of his terms and a point below where it stood two weeks earlier.
The same Reuters/Ipsos survey had Democrats ahead of Republicans 47% to 35% on the generic congressional ballot, a 12-point gap that was the widest of the election cycle.
The administration's immigration policies, including deportations by ICE due to strengthened funding via the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, were also scrutinized.

Polling found that Hispanics, who were considered a key reason for Trump's victory in the 2024 election, overwhelmingly disapproved of Trump and had largely swung back towards Democrats due to economic concerns and dissatisfaction of Trump's handling of immigration and deportation.

An October Reuters/Ipsos poll found that majorities said the cost of living was their top issue for the election and that 76% of Americans blamed Trump's policies for increasing inflation, including 57% of Republicans.
Signs of an enthusiasm gap between Republican and Democratic voters were noted by analysts as possibly forecasting a Democratic "blue wave".

In September 2026, American political analyst Charlie Cook described this phenomenon as a "red undertow", arguing that anticipated Democratic victories would come not from a rising Democratic tide, but a drowning Trump brand.

A month before the election, polling consistently found that Democratic candidates were leading key races for state governorships and those that would determine control of the Senate, with large swings towards Democratic candidates by independent voters.

The New York Times highlighted how Kansas, a state that had not elected a Democratic Senator since the Great Depression, had become a competitive battleground amid an unexpected surge of Democratic support deep in Republican territory.

Furthermore, a poll commissioned by The Washington Post and George Mason University had to deal with the unusual issue of far fewer Republicans (12%) willing to respond than Democrats (32%), an exceptional gap.
Democratic support came amidst multiple polls finding record-low approval ratings for Trump which some analysts considered was negatively impacting down-ballot races.
Trump repeatedly told voters to pretend he was on the ballot to increase Republican enthusiasm.
Both Democrats and some analysts considered this instruction to voters a mistake, due to Trump's low approval ratings.
Increasing concerns about the Republicans' position in the November midterm elections have exposed tensions within Donald Trump's political structure.
According to Reuters, Trump criticized his advisers for their election strategy, including decisions related to campaign spending and candidate selection.
This is despite polls suggesting that Democrats could gain control of the House of Representatives.

In October, the Trump administration called for Ukraine to replace Volodymyr Zelenskyy as the nation's president and struck a deal with Russia to purchase the country's fuel in an effort to bring down diesel prices before the elections, and deepened Russian-American cooperation.

The fuel deal was criticized by Democrats and some Republicans for undercutting the Lindsey O. Graham Sanctioning Russia and Iran Act of 2026, which allowed the president to waive tariffs or sanctions if he certified to Congress that doing so was in the national interest of the United States.
Some Democratic lawmakers were concerned about Trump unilaterally lifting the sanctions against Russia, justifying their opposition to the bill.
Julian E. Zelizer has drawn a comparison between the 1966 and 2026 midterm elections.
Writing for Foreign Policy in October 2026, he noted that the Republican campaign of 1966 focused on the economic cost of the Vietnam War, including growing federal deficits and inflation.
He argued that the economic impact of the war in Iran, which had driven consumer prices up, gave Democrats an opening similar to the one Republicans had seized in 1966.

Zelizer acknowledged that the Iran war had not reached the scale of Vietnam and likely never would, but said its economic effects had nonetheless been considerable—and in some respects clearer—and that the war had been unpopular from the outset.
Political analyst Natalie Jackson told Al Jazeera that the polling pointed to a "pretty favourable" environment for Democrats.

She traced this to public frustration with Trump and the economy—high costs driven in part by tariffs and the war in Iran—and said the prevailing mood was that Republicans had failed to deliver over the past two years.
Foreign nations have sought to interfere with the 2026 elections.
Since 2016, "the Kremlin has initiated online influence operations in every American federal election cycle" according to declassified intelligence documents.

According to US intelligence officials, in 2026, Russia is targeting Americans with covert online disinformation campaigns to undermine confidence in the election and seed and promote domestic divisions with the goal to "inject chaos".
No evidence exists that Russia has attempted to take aim at voting machinery or compromise the voting process.

US intelligence officials have described the effort as less extensive and coordinated than prior years, with officials speculating Russia is less interested in midterm races than presidential contests and is distracted by the Russo-Ukrainian war.

US intelligence has speculated Iran may have engaged in online influence efforts, and in August 2026 Meta Platforms reported a small number of accounts on Facebook and Instagram originating from Iran spreading AI generated content with "anti-Republican views".
US intelligence speculates that unlike prior years where China supported or opposed individual candidates based on their views, it may stay out of the 2026 elections due to fears of blowback.
On October 14, 2026, the social network X suspended more than 13,000 accounts linked to Iran, Russia, and China ahead of the US midterm elections.
According to Graphika, social media accounts linked to Chinese government influence operation Spamouflage posed as U.S. voters to post divisive content.

In a prime time address on July 16, Trump alleged (among other things) that China had collected 220 million American voter identification files including private information in 2022 and that it amounted to election interference.
Trump then declassified intelligence records he presented as evidence the US election system falls "catastrophically short".

Election experts pushed back on some of the claims, stating that voter registration files are public and easily accessible in most states and would not necessarily allow interference with the voting process.

On September 28, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth announced the Department of Defense would launch an effort dedicated to combating foreign meddling in US elections that would use "advanced intelligence and cyber capabilities to identify, disrupt, and neutralize foreign interference".
Democratic leaders of the House and Senate intelligence committees have expressed worry that Trump will use claims of foreign interference in an attempt to intervene in the midterm elections.
An analysis of political advertising related to the Iran war found that 61 of the 65 ads examined between September 1 and October 14, 2026, focused on the cost of living.
The ads aired more than 43,000 times on television, with an estimated total expenditure of $42 million.

In January 2026, The Washington Post reported that the second Trump administration had undertaken several tactics, including mid-decade redrawing of congressional districts for partisan gain, prosecution of political opponents, and a push to change voting methods and rules, that were meant to undermine confidence in the midterm elections.

In October 2026, a New York Times analysis found Trump had attacked the integrity of US elections more than 70% of the days since he returned to office, particularly with false claims about "rigged" voting machines and fraudulent mail-in ballots.
Upon returning to office, the Trump administration has dismantled election security efforts across the federal government.

Such cuts have included: firing or reassigning personnel at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency focused on elections; defunding training programs for the Elections Infrastructure Information Sharing and Analysis Center; eliminating the FBI's foreign influence taskforce; downsizing and announcing closure of the Foreign Malign Influence Center; and firing all members of the independent Election Assistance Commission.
Trump appointed prominent 2020 election deniers into positions in government that could oversee the voting process.

In the lead up to the election, pro-Trump conspiracy theorists and election deniers have won local races responsible for overseeing election results, and several election deniers are running for electoral offices in battleground states.
In March, the House of Representatives passed the SAVE America Act, an amended version of the previously proposed Safeguard American Voter Eligibility Act.
The bill, if approved by the Senate and signed into law by Trump, would have required voters to provide proof of citizenship in order to obtain or renew their voter registration.
Voting rights experts said that such provisions would disenfranchise married women, racial minorities, low-income groups, and people who legally changed their name, among others.
The bill ultimately died in the Senate that June, with four Republicans joining Democrats to block its inclusion.
In January, Trump floated the idea of illegally canceling the elections, citing an expected loss in the elections and a distrust in democratic systems.
White House Press Secretary Karoline Leavitt later stated that Trump was "speaking facetiously", and was "simply joking".
In February, Trump stated that the elections should be nationalized to prevent voter fraud.

On February 27, The Washington Post reported that several right-wing activists are working with the Trump administration to draft an executive order which, if signed, would effectively instate a national emergency and give Trump extended powers over the elections.
Trump denied the existence of such an order.
According to ABC News, Trump met prominent election denier Tina Peters on October 5 at the White House.

Speaking to conservative podcaster Joe Oltmann on October 8, Peters' attorney stated that Trump "is not going to relinquish control again" if he believes the elections are rigged, and that "It's better—if we're going to have a civil war of any sort—that it be martial law with our side in control of the armaments."

sentences.section: Concerns over ICE at polling places
sentences.text: In February, Steve Bannon said the federal government was planning to send ICE to patrol polling stations in an attempt to prevent a Democratic victory, vowing to "never again allow an election to be stolen".

sentences.text: In March, Stateline reported that legislation to "restrict immigration enforcement or the presence of federal forces" near polling places and other election sites has been offered or announced in California, Connecticut, New Mexico, Pennsylvania, Rhode Island, Virginia and Washington.

sentences.section: Concerns over ICE at polling places
sentences.text: The same month, the Associated Press reported that several Democratic-led states including New Mexico and Virginia were taking steps to counter potential tactics to intimidate voters.

sentences.section: Concerns over ICE at polling places

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: Internal documents reviewed by The New York Times found a widespread effort by the federal government to promote mistrust in the integrity of the 2026 election, with Department of Homeland Security officials investigating over 150 nonprofit organizations they alleged were helping noncitizens to vote.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: Trump and Republicans have repeatedly made false and unsubstantiated claims of massive voter fraud by noncitizens, with The Times describing Trump as making the case that "any Democratic election victory is suspicious on its face".

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: As part of investigations into election-integrity, the Justice Department has demanded voter registration data from states, suing 23 states and the District of Columbia that declined to provide unredacted voter rolls; all of the sued states were led by Democrats or had been won by Joe Biden in 2020.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: In January 2026, a federal judge blocked the Trump administration from threatening to withhold election funding from states that did not provide their voter information or alter their voter registration forms or voter systems.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: Also in January 2026, U.S. District Judge David Carter dismissed the department's lawsuit against California, which had sought personal information including partial Social Security numbers for roughly 23 million registered voters, ruling that the demands violated privacy laws and writing that federal centralization of the data would have a "chilling effect" on voter registration; a federal judge dismissed a similar lawsuit against Oregon later that month.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: The department appealed the California ruling to the Ninth Circuit.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: In June 2026, federal prosecutors in Los Angeles publicly accused the state of blocking a voter roll audit and said they were conducting election fraud investigations while ballots from the state's June primary were still being counted.

sentences.text: The Department of Homeland Security engaged in a widespread effort to investigate supposed voter fraud.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: Per internal documents released by the advocacy group Democracy Forward, efforts have relied on the Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) division of Immigration and Customs Enforcement, which CNN described as part of a "phased national initiative involving voter-roll acquisition, data analysis, investigative leads and field investigations".

sentences.text: Ahead of the elections, Trump made false claims of voter fraud through mail-in ballots, calling it "corrupt" and "cheating", and encouraged Republican lawmakers to pass strict voter ID laws claiming it would "guarantee the midterms" for the GOP.

sentences.text: In March 2026, Trump signed a new executive order on elections which would require the government to compile a list of eligible voters in each state and only allow the United States Post Office to send ballots to verified voters.

sentences.text: On September 14, the Supreme Court ruled against the Trump administration's attempt to screen mail-in ballots finding the government was "unlikely to succeed on the merits" and that it would implement chaos and confusion ahead of the elections.

sentences.text: Following the ruling, state election officials were described as moving to restore faith in mail-in voting, and Trump later encouraged Republicans to vote by mail.

sentences.text: The Trump administration had overhauled the system to combine social security and other data to create a master database of citizens per Executive Order 14248.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: On October 22, 2026, Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín of the Northern District of California issued preliminary injunction that bars the Department of Homeland Security from conducting election-related field operations in California, Connecticut, Georgia, Missouri, Nevada, New York, Pennsylvania, Washington, and Wisconsin until the polls close on Election Day (November 3, 2026).

sentences.text: On October 26, 2026, President Donald Trump announced a $1 million reward for information on voter fraud in past elections or the 2026 midterms, to be paid if the tip led to an arrest and conviction.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud

sentences.text: The letters, signed by Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter, did not cite a specific violation or investigation.

sentences.text: Justin Levitte, a former justice department official, said the letter looked "meant to intimidate rather than to infom," while election law professor Joshua Douglas said he had never seen the department send such a letter nationwide days before an election.

sentences.text: The war with Iran became a subject of Democratic campaigning ahead of the November 3 midterm elections.

sentences.text: On October 24, former president Barack Obama criticized Trump's decision to launch the war during a rally in Cleveland supporting Democratic Senate candidate Sherrod Brown and gubernatorial candidate Amy Acton.

sentences.section: Federal investigations and false claims of voter fraud
sentences.text: Obama described the conflict as unnecessary and criticized the administration's foreign policy, urging voters to use the midterm elections to challenge the direction of the Trump administration.

In January 2026, FBI agents executed a search warrant at the Fulton County, Georgia, election center, seizing approximately 600 boxes of ballots and other records from the 2020 presidential election, an action election law experts described as unprecedented federal intervention in locally administered elections.

Federal investigations of the 2020 election subsequently expanded to several states: the Office of the Director of National Intelligence procured voting machines in Puerto Rico for examination in February, federal officials subpoenaed records of the partisan review of Maricopa County, Arizona's 2020 results in March, the Justice Department demanded ballots cast in Wayne County, Michigan, in April, and FBI agents questioned former poll workers in Milwaukee, Wisconsin, in May.

David Becker, executive director of The Center for Election Innovation & Research, said the investigations were "about the 2026 and 2028 elections" rather than 2020, characterizing them as intimidation of election officials.

John Keller, former acting head of the Justice Department's Public Integrity Section, said the administration appeared to be normalizing federal investigation of state elections in preparation for potentially challenging future results.

In June 2026, FBI agents searched the Cleveland offices of the Ohio Organizing Collaborative, a voter registration and community organizing group, seizing computers and questioning staff and volunteers across Ohio as part of a Justice Department investigation into the group's voter registration efforts; the Brennan Center for Justice said the search fit a pattern of federal inquiries targeting voting infrastructure ahead of the midterm elections.

Five weeks before the midterm elections, the Department of Homeland Security allocated $20M in taxpayer funds initially reserved for Customs and Border Protection from the One Big Beautiful Bill Act to air campaign-style television ads promoting Donald Trump, drawing widespread bipartisan criticism.
The White House defended the ads as "public service announcements" aimed at promoting patriotism rather than campaigning.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters, "I like the message, but it shouldn't be paid for with taxpayer money."
Multiple legal experts contacted by the Associated Press said the advertisements likely violated federal law prohibiting "publicity or propaganda."
Following widespread criticism, Trump announced he would pay for the ads via a campaign account, but did not commit to reimbursing the government the $12M already spent on the ad campaign.

On October 11, a federal judge issued an order to stop the airing of Trump administration television advertisements funded by taxpayer money, but two other advertisements were also broadcast after the deadline set by the court.
The next day, Justice Department lawyers apologized for the incident, saying that legal counsel had not been informed of the court's order in time.
Overall, advertising spending for the 2026 midterm elections surpassed $10 billion by the middle of October.
Since July, Elon Musk has spent more than $276 million on right-wing political groups to help maintain the Republican majority.
With total spending of about $366 million, he has become the largest donor in the 2026 U.S. midterm elections.

The donations include $158 million to the Senate Leadership Fund, the largest supporter of Republican Senate candidates, $76 million to America PAC, and $10 million to Lone Star Liberty PAC, which supports Ken Paxton, the Republican Senate candidate in Texas, running against Democratic candidate James Talarico.
As the 2026 election entered its final stages, spending by super PACs and dark money reached record levels.
Hundreds of millions of dollars have been paid by major donors to influence government policy, with the largest donors tending to lean more toward the Republican Party.
Public anger over the role of money in politics has been growing, and both parties promised to fight corruption if they win.
By law, super PACs must operate independently of candidates, but in practice, candidates and these groups have often worked in close coordination.
For example, Trump has repeatedly referred to funds raised by the super PAC "MAGA Inc." as his own money.

Less than five years after entering U.S. political campaigns, the American Israel Public Affairs Committee (AIPAC) has raised $233 million, making it one of the best-funded groups in midterm elections.
It has also become polarizing, however, with many candidates rejecting its support, and some even highlighting opposition to AIPAC as a point of pride.
AIPAC faces criticism and calls itself part of a bigger struggle to protect Israel.
Despite challenges and shifting public opinion, AIPAC plans to continue spending heavily on campaigns.
AIPAC has invested over $54 million in U.S. congressional races through its super PAC, the United Democracy Project (UDP), making it the largest outside spender in the current election cycle.
Despite some victories, AIPAC faced significant setbacks, such as in Michigan, where its funding failed to secure a win for its favored candidate.
Critics argue that AIPAC's influence is waning, as many voters, especially Democrats, believe the U.S. is too supportive of Israel.
This shift in public opinion has led to discomfort among Republicans as well.
AIPAC's financial power remains strong, contributing $30 million to UDP.
Despite this, AIPAC has become less favorable among candidates and voters across the political spectrum, especially younger people.
Many candidates preferred not to mention AIPAC or its funding in their campaigns, recognizing its potential negative impact.

During this midterms cycle, AIPAC's strategy appeared to shift due to negative voter perception linked to Israel's actions in Gaza and U.S. military aid towards Israel, focusing on funding other groups and uniting donors rather than directly endorsing candidates.
Political analyst Trita Parsi noted AIPAC's previous power was fading, as its name is now viewed negatively.
AIPAC also planned to invest in Republican candidate Mike Rogers in Michigan, trying to defeat Democratic candidate Abdul El-Sayed who had been critical of the organization.
During the 2026 US midterm elections, betting on election outcomes on prediction platforms such as Polymarket and Kalshi has increased significantly.

According to a Reuters report on October 14, 2026, an analysis by the Anti-Corruption Data Collective (ACDC) shows that trading volume in these platforms' election markets has exceeded $220 million, while the figure was about $92 million in the 2024 congressional elections.
Kalshi and Polymarket have partnered with various news organisations for election coverage.
For instance, in December 2025, Kalshi partnered with CNN in order to include their data in news coverage.
A similar deal was struck between Polymarket and Yahoo finance.

On October 23, 2026, President Trump announced he had personally requested the Department of Justice to file a lawsuit arguing that the 2026 Senate election in Alaska should not be certified if Democrat Mary Peltola wins.

The filing's justification is that the appearance on the ballot of two similarly named candidates – incumbent Republican senator Dan S. Sullivan and independent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. – may lead to voter confusion.
J. Sullivan Jr. was previously affirmed by the state's Supreme Court to appear on the ballot when state election officials made allegations that his candidacy was an intended spoiler.
The federal suit was dismissed by U.S. District Court Judge Sharon Gleason on November 1.

On October 28, Alaska Governor Mike Dunleavy announced a state criminal investigation into Peltola's campaign after the New York Times reported staffers may have intentionally recruited candidates such as J. Sullivan Jr. to be spoilers.
On October 30 it was revealed that a federal investigation has been underway "for several months" already.
In September 2026, Trump barred CNN, MS NOW, and Politico from the White House grounds.
The three outlets filed suit, arguing that the ban violated due process and First Amendment protections.
The move drew criticism from Republican strategists, who warned that it diverted attention from economic issues ahead of the midterms.

The lead-up to the elections was marked by an inflation surge amidst affordability concerns, particularly on gas, healthcare, and food prices, exacerbated by the Trump administration's tariffs and Strait of Hormuz crisis caused by the 2026 Iran War.

The growth of artificial intelligence became an unexpected issue, with voters concerned about AI-induced mass unemployment, its environmental impacts, mass surveillance, and the risk of human extinction from a hypothetically developed superintelligence.
Income inequality, democratic backsliding, corruption, and foreign policy were frequently cited among voters in exit polling.
Trump made threats of annexing multiple countries and used executive orders to change the names of Lake Ontario ("Lake America") and the Gulf of Mexico ("Gulf of America").
Polling by Harvard University found that youth were "deeply concerned about the country's future" and under fiscal stress.

Just 9% found the country to be going in a positive direction, a large majority were worried about AI-driven job displacement, 88% labeled endemic corruption in the United States important to their vote, and a plurality believes that they will "be worse off financially than their parents".
The Democratic Party leads 63% to 26% among likely voters.
The economy, including gas prices, inflation, healthcare, tariffs, and cost of living, is one of the primary issues of the election.

The second Trump administration imposed the largest tax increase in American history in April 2025, with an expected six trillion dollars in returned taxation if maintained until 2035, on much of the world with the intent to re-industrialize the United States.
It was criticized by experts and global leaders for worsening inflation.
Fuel costs were increased by the 2026 Iran war.
The Trump administration announced in October 2026 that it would buy diesel from Russia and suspend sanctions on Russian diesel until April 2027.
The move was intended to lower fuel prices before the November elections.
A group of seven senators—four Republicans and three Democrats—criticized the decision.
They said it violates the 2022 congressional ban on Russian energy imports.
They also said the administration neither consulted Congress nor gave the required legal justification.
At the same time, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent defended the agreement, saying the government was acting under existing legal authority and that the deal would reduce prices.
Trade, including tariffs, was a leading issue of the campaign season.
Data released on October 14, 2026, by the Bureau of Labor Statistics showed US annual inflation rising to 3.7 per cent in September.
That marked an increase from 3.4 per cent in August and exceeded the 3.6 per cent forecast by economists in a Bloomberg poll.
It was the first uptick since May.
Core inflation, which leaves out food and energy, also surpassed Wall Street expectations, climbing to 2.6 per cent from 2.4 per cent the month before.
In the final weeks before the elections, the Trump administration pledged to provide U.S. farmers and ranchers with an agricultural aid and bailout package worth more than $15 billion.

The programs, which include an $8 billion Harvest Fuel Relief Program to offset high diesel and operating costs, were criticized by political analysts who describe the timing as targeted electoral outreach while also receiving support for stabilizing rural economies.
Inequality in the United States continued to increase.
There is increasing support for a universal healthcare system, with the nation having a far lower lifespan than comparable wealthy countries.
The United States is one of a few wealthy democracies without a universal healthcare system.

A survey that was conducted by Harvard University found that more than "two-thirds of young Americans (68%) view the power of large corporations as a serious threat to their long-term financial security, while 62% say the same about the wealth and power of billionaires.
Concern about corporate power crosses party lines, including 81% of young Democrats, 67% of Independents, and 60% of Republicans.
They also wrote on November 3, 2026 that "Support for Medicare for All and a wealth tax points to an economic populist thread that extends beyond young Democrats.
Majorities favor creating a national health insurance program (57%) and establishing a 2% annual tax on household wealth above $50 million (54%).
Both proposals receive majority support among Democrats (75% and 70%, respectively) and independents (55% and 52%), along with support from roughly four in ten Republicans (39% and 42%)."
According to a September 2026 Gallup poll, 89% of people believe that there is pervasive corruption within the US government.
While in office, Trump has engaged in unprecedented self-enrichment and faced widespread allegations of corruption.
Trump's grants of pardons and clemency have favored political allies and loyalists, with several given after millions in donations or fees.
Trump has proactively solicited donations from companies and individuals following which favorable regulatory actions and decisions have occurred.
He has maintained an active stock market account with thousands of trades totaling hundreds of millions of dollars.

Trump has directly benefited by soliciting his own memecoin, $TRUMP and from his family's cryptocurrency company World Liberty Financial which has received investments by anonymous individuals and foreign governments.
According to analysis from The New York Times, anonymous political contributions to the midterm elections, known as "dark money," exceeded $1 billion by late August.
This funding is funneled into Super PACs through nonprofit organizations and shell companies, allowing donors to remain undisclosed.
The United States has suffered from political dysfunction and immense erosion in democratic health.
Polling has indicated that voters are afraid of the nation becoming authoritarian.

The large majority of Americans favor major changes to the nation's political system, including abolishing the electoral college and replacing it with a direct popular vote, implementing campaign spending limits, and enacting age limits for the Supreme Court of the United States.
The Senate has also become a subject for reform, and according to The Week is one of the "most unloved institutions" in the country.

The second Trump administration was hallmarked by a massive increase in funding and power for the agencies United States Customs and Border Protection and United States Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
The agencies conducted raids and throughout mostly Democratic cities, resulting in the killings of protestors Alex Pretti and Renee Good.
The government used the Alien Enemies Act to deport both non-citizens and citizens.
Many protestors and politicians adopted the slogan "Abolish ICE."
These actions disproportionally affected Latinos.
In 2024, Latinos, especially Latino men, supported Donald Trump's re-election much more than previous Republican candidates.
By 2026, largely due to issues caused by this enforcement, this support had evaporated.
Artificial intelligence (AI) became a leading concern for voters.
Opposition to water, energy, and pollution–intensive data centers, and AI more broadly, emerged as an unexpected issue during the election.
The Brookings Institution described the backlash as part of a broader opposition against "AI power".

Republicans in the election generally took stances in the midterm more favorable to Silicon Valley, the construction of data centers, and the future of AI development than Democratic candidates, although the issue was not as partisanized as others.
Concerns included widespread unemployment through artificial general intelligence's development, imposition of mass surveillance, and the existential risk of superintelligence to humanity.

A bipartisan group in Congress of conservatives, liberals, socialists, and populists has united in opposition to transhumanist and post-humanist ideals in AI development, including Republican senator Josh Hawley, right-wing populist Steve Bannon, Democratic representative Greg Casar, and independent senator Bernie Sanders.
On September 29, 2026, President Trump signed an executive order to replace the term artificial intelligence with super intelligence (SI) in official communications and documents.
The order mandates all government agencies to use this terminology, including for technologies that do not fit the accepted definition of superintelligence.
According to Harvard, "Nearly two-thirds of young Americans (64%) see AI replacing jobs as a serious threat to their financial security.
Concern crosses party lines: 76% of young Democrats and 61% of both Republicans and independents regard it as a serious threat."
A September 2026 poll found that 70% of Americans oppose data center construction in their own communities.
AI opposition has occurred across bipartisan lines, described as "sweeping the globe" by Politico.
A September 2026 Quinnipac University poll found that 73% of Americans "would oppose the building of an AI data center in their community" while 21% would support it.
The Trump administration has implemented mass surveillance in the United States through the development of artificial intelligence technologies.
Flock cameras and other video surveillance have been rapidly constructed on American streets since the beginning of his term, with Trump saying that "I like them" in September 2026.
There have been arguments made that the U.S. is taking on the characteristics of a surveillance state.
Democrats have called for stricter privacy laws modeled on the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation.
Republicans have generally believed that mass survelliance improves safety, and that individuals should be willing to give up aspects of privacy in return for protection.

President Trump and the Republican Party campaigned on changing terminology for emerging technologies and geographic landmarks, including the Gulf of Mexico, New Mexico, artificial intelligence, and the Atlantic Ocean.
In May 2025, Republicans passed a bill in the House of Representatives to rename the "Gulf of Mexico" to the "Gulf of America".
The Trump administration and Republicans have used it to portray Democrats as unpatriotic.
A major topic on the election campaign trail was the 2026 Iran war.
The war was preceded by the largest US military buildup in the region since the 2003 invasion of Iraq.
It resulted in thousands of civilian and military casualties.
The economic impact of the war included the largest supply disruption of the global oil market, disruptions of the natural gas, fertilizer, aviation, and tourism industries, and financial volatility.
, the US Department of Defense estimated that the war had so far cost $47.1 billion.

American rationale for initiating the war included regime change, preventing Iran from obtaining a nuclear weapon, a response to the massacre of anti-government protesters in Iran, and seizing Iran's resources.
Critics have rejected these justifications, stating that the attack is a war of aggression and illegal.
Initially setting upon a course to overthrow the Iranian government, later goals focused on nuclear negotiations and reopening the Strait of Hormuz.
Public opinion was mostly opposed to the war in the U.S. and in many other countries, leading to disapproval for Donald Trump and declining views of the US and Israel around the world.

Also, according to two polls conducted by Fox News and the Associated Press-NORC between October 8 and 12, 2026, the Iran war has become one of the most important concerns for voters in the midterm elections, surpassing immigration and crime.
A Fox News poll showed that 60% of voters opposed US military action against Iran and preferred Democratic congressional candidates.
After Republicans' losses in the midterm election, Trump acknowledged that the Iran war had played a role in the defeat.
According to a report in The Atlantic on November 1, 2026, Trump is considering resuming military strikes on Iran.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: Since Pope Leo XIV's election as Pope in 2025, the Trump administration has made direct attacks on the Pope, the Catholic Church, and the Holy See that were described by scholars as historically unparalleled by any Western government.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: The issue saw widespread attention during the election, and Mainline Protestants, Catholics, and evangelical Protestants shifted by double-digits in polling towards Independent and Democratic candidates, alleging that Trump's policies, behavior, and political agenda were in direct contradiction to the tenets of Christian morality.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: After genocidal threats were made by Donald Trump to Iran on April 7 saying "a whole civilization will die", Pope Leo XIV called for peace.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: On April 12, 2026, President Donald Trump directly criticized the pope in a Truth Social post, writing that "Pope Leo is WEAK on Crime, and terrible for Foreign Policy," and "catering to the Radical Left".

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: Marco Politi, a long time Vatican observer and author, stated: "You have to jump back to the Middle Ages when kings and emperors were shouting against the pope in Rome and calling him false.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: There is just no other recent example like this."

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: Academic Andrew Chestnut stated, "I cannot think of any parallels, at least coming from Western Christian majority countries, of such pointed and public attacks on the Pope."

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See
sentences.text: Another dispute between the Holy See and the Trump administration emerged in the last two weeks of the midterm election, after "12 clergymen joined Trump on Thursday in the Oval Office", for what Archbishop Jeffrey Grob of Milwaukee has said was intended to be a private meeting to discuss matters such as "immigration enforcement, religious worker visas, and human dignity" but was falsely portrayed by the administration as a midterm religious endorsement.

sentences.section: Religious conflicts, rift with the Holy See

sentences.text: Pope Leo XIV, who retained his American citizenship after becoming pontiff, voted by mail in the midterm election for his home state of Illinois, becoming the first pope to vote in a secular election.

Compared to previous US elections, the 2026 elections saw sharply less focus on China, with AdImpact estimating 44 different television ads criticizing China this election cycle, compared to 190 before the 2022 elections and 216 before the 2024 presidential election.
The group also estimated spending on those ads totaled at $26.2 million, decreasing from $65.6 million in 2022 and $119.1 million in 2024.
It estimated that Republicans accounted for 86% of this election's anti-China ads.
In contrast, Democrats produced six such ads, all by House candidates and none by Senate ones; in 2024, Democrats ran 81 such ads.

Analysts have attributed the declining focus on China on President Trump's focus on improving relations with the country, China as an issue being crowded by domestic and foreign concerns such as the Iran war, as well as relatively improving views of China among Americans.
Thirty-five seats in the United States Senate were up for election, including all 33 Class 2 seats.
Republicans gained majority control of the Senate in the 2024 elections by flipping four Democratic seats.

Two Democratic-held seats up for election, Georgia and Michigan, were in states won by Donald Trump in the previous presidential election, while Maine was the only Republican-held seat up for election in a state won by Kamala Harris.
Democrats won control of the Senate in 2026, defending every Democratic-held seat up for election and picking up several seats in Republican-leaning territory.

Adam Hamilton became the first Democrat to win a Senate election in Kansas since 1932, while James Talarico of Texas, Annie Andrews of South Carolina, Sherrod Brown of Ohio, Josh Turek of Iowa, and Roy Cooper of North Carolina all won Senate seats in states that Trump had won in 2024.

Reacting to these victories, Nate Cohn noted that "[t]here's simply no modern precedent for either party to do so well in states that had leaned so heavily toward the other side," highlighting Democratic victories in Kansas and Texas as especially significant due to their traditional Republican lean.
Additionally, in Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson defeated five-term incumbent Susan Collins.
Two special elections were held to fill the unexpired terms of senators who vacated their seats during the :
Florida Class 3: Republican Marco Rubio resigned his seat on January 20, 2025, to become U.S. secretary of state under the second Trump administration.
Ashley Moody was appointed by Florida governor Ron DeSantis to fill the seat until the special election, which took place concurrently with the regularly scheduled 2026 elections.
Ohio Class 3: Republican JD Vance resigned his seat on January 10, 2025, following his election as vice president of the United States.
Jon Husted was appointed by Ohio governor Mike DeWine to fill the seat until the special election, which took place concurrently with the regularly scheduled 2026 elections.
All 435 voting seats in the United States House of Representatives were up for election.

Additionally, elections were held to select the non-voting delegate for the District of Columbia and the non-voting delegates from 4 of the 5 U.S. territories, excluding Puerto Rico due to its non-voting delegate serving a 4-year term.
There are 16 Democratic incumbents in districts Donald Trump won, while only 8 Republican incumbents are in seats won by Harris.

The House map featured a number of new congressional maps: Ohio and Utah had new, court-mandated congressional districts this cycle; Missouri, North Carolina, and Texas redrew their maps mid-cycle; and the district map was changed in California following the passage of Prop 50.
In Missouri, the legality of a Republican-backed congressional map remained disputed in September 2026.
On September 8, Supreme Court Justice Brett Kavanaugh declined to intervene in an emergency appeal seeking to allow the new map to be used in the November election.

Hours later, U.S. District Judge Stephen Clark issued a temporary order requiring Missouri to use the Republican-backed map, conflicting with Missouri Supreme Court ruling that had blocked its use and ordered a referendum on the map.
The competing rulings left the state's congressional districts unresolved ahead of the general election.

However, on September 10, the U.S. Supreme Court stayed Judge Clark's order whilst a federal lawsuit filed by Republican nominees Bob Onder and Rick Brattin for the 3rd and 5th districts respectively, played out.

The United States Court of Appeals for the Eighth Circuit then fast-tracked the case for a hearing on September 17 and, ruling on the merits, affirmed the lower courts order on September 21, remanding the case back to the District Court for entry of a permanent injunction but stayed their ruling for a week pending an appeal to the U.S. Supreme Court.

On September 25, the U.S. Supreme Court unanimously held that state law rules in the case and granted an emergency stay of the Eighth Circuit's order and Judge Clark's injunction, leaving the 2022 maps in place for the 2026 elections.

The court also faulted the District Court and the Eighth Circuit for what it deemed as having "incorrectly applied" the Purcell Principle and further held that the Supreme Court of Missouri was not at fault for "upsetting the status quo".
Democrats won control of the House of Representatives in 2026, winning numerous races across the country, including in districts that had voted for Trump by a large margin in 2024.
Six special elections to the House of Representatives were held in 2026.
Texas's 18th congressional district: Democrat Christian Menefee defeated fellow Democrat Amanda Edwards in a runoff to succeed Democrat Sylvester Turner, who died on March 5, 2025.
The district has a partisan index of D+21.
Georgia's 14th congressional district: Republican Clay Fuller defeated Democrat Shawn Harris in a runoff to succeed Republican Marjorie Taylor Greene, who resigned on January 5, 2026.
The district has a partisan index of R+19.

New Jersey's 11th congressional district: Democrat Analilia Mejia defeated Republican Joe Hathaway to succeed Democrat Mikie Sherrill, who resigned on November 20, 2025, to take office as governor of New Jersey.
The district has a partisan index of D+5.
California's 1st congressional district: Republican James Gallagher defeated Democrats Audrey Denney and Mike McGuire to succeed Republican Doug LaMalfa, who died on January 6, 2026.
The district has a partisan index of R+12.

California's 14th congressional district: Democrat Aisha Wahab defeated fellow Democrat Melissa Hernandez in a runoff to succeed Democrat Eric Swalwell, who resigned on April 14, 2026, following accusations of sexual misconduct.
The district has a partisan index of D+20.
Georgia's 13th congressional district: Democrat Everton Blair defeated fellow Democrat Marcye Scott in a runoff to succeed Democrat David Scott, who died on April 22, 2026.
This district has a partisan index of D+21.
36 states and three territories held regularly scheduled gubernatorial elections.
The governors of 15 states and two territories were term-limited.
Prior to the 2026 gubernatorial elections, Republicans controlled 26 of the 50 state governorships, and each party held 18 state governorships up for election.
Republicans had held a majority of the state governorships since the 2010 elections.
Democrats won control of a majority of U.S. state governorships in the 2026 gubernatorial elections, in part due to a series of victories in Republican-leaning states.
Democrats swept every statewide race in Texas, with Gina Hinojosa becoming the first Democrat to win the Texas gubernatorial election since the 1990 Texas gubernatorial election.
Keisha Lance Bottoms won the Georgia gubernatorial election, the first Democrat to do so since the 1998 Georgia gubernatorial election.
Amy Acton in Ohio and Rob Sand in Iowa became the first Democrats to win their respective states since the 2006 elections.
In Nevada, Democrat Aaron Ford defeated Joe Lombardo, ending four years of Republican control of the office.
One major exception to Democratic gains was the state of Florida, where Republicans retained majorities in the state legislature and Republican Byron Donalds won the gubernatorial election.
Nine states held lieutenant gubernatorial elections independently from their gubernatorial elections.
30 states, two territories, and one federal district held regularly scheduled attorney general elections.
26 states held regularly scheduled secretary of state elections.
27 states held regularly scheduled treasurer elections.
23 states held regularly scheduled auditor elections.
88 state legislative chambers and 5 territorial chambers held regularly scheduled elections.
Republicans have held a majority of the state legislative chambers and seats since the 2010 elections.
Prior to the regularly-scheduled 2026 state legislative elections, Republicans hold 4044 state legislative seats, while Democrats hold 3227 state legislative seats.

Democrats flipped at least one legislative chamber in each of Michigan, Minnesota, Pennsylvania, and Wisconsin, gaining trifectas (unified control of the governorship and both legislative chambers) in each state.

They also gained a trifecta in Nevada by winning the gubernatorial race and retaining control of both of Nevada's legislative chambers, and broke a Republican trifecta in Texas by winning the governorship and the Texas House of Representatives.
Democrats also won a majority in the North Carolina House of Representatives and made legislative gains in several other states, including Iowa, Missouri, and Ohio.
Elections were held in 2026, in various states across the country, including supreme courts and appellate courts.
100 ballot measures in 37 states were held in the November election.
Local elections will be held in the United States throughout 2026 to elect officers of municipal and county governments.

At least 22 mayorships in the country's top 100 most populous cities will be up for election, and many more will hold elections for local ballot measures, city council, and numerous other municipal offices.
Many of these races will coincide with the 2026 midterm elections.
A number of major cities will hold mayoral elections in 2026.

The results were labeled a rebuke of President Trump, Trumpism and further AI development.
Analysts called the election results "a fundamental realignment" in American politics unparalleled since the post-Watergate Era.

Axios said that "Make no mistake: Democrats won by epic, sometimes historic margins across red and blue states, up and down ballots, obliterating almost everything President Trump, and a Republican Party remade wholly in his image, built over the past decade in American politics."
Democrats won the largest popular-vote victory in the House of Representatives since 1976 in a lopsided electoral rout labeled a "Blue Tsunami".

Statistician Nate Silver said that "the election could accelerate a shift away from the political era Trump has dominated for more than a decade and toward a new debate over who leads both parties, and how the country responds to AI-driven change."
Peter Baker said it was "the beginning of the end to the Trump era" while The New York Times said that it left Trump as "a Lame Duck with two years left to fight".
Fox News's Sean Hannity, a prominent Trump supporter, said: "Hatred is a hell of a motivator.
I think the hatred for this man [Trump] is unprecedented.
I’ve never seen anything like it."

NBC News reported the Democratic Party "won historic electoral victories Tuesday night on a pledge to make life more affordable for Americans, an issue that united voters across political and demographic divides" and the "stunning electoral results on Tuesday night were the culmination of a months long effort by Democrats to make the high cost of living a central campaign issue in races across the country up and down the ballot".

NBC News exit polls found that 70% believed that Congress was not doing "enough to provide checks and balances on the presidency" and that that the U.S. economic system generally "favors the wealthy".
69% of voters believed the country's economic system favors the wealthy, while only 31% said it is generally fair.
A majority predicted that life for the next generation of Americans would be worse and that AI was likely to "do more to hurt society" than help.
Most said that the cost of living, the war in Iran, government corruption, ICE, data centers, and AI were "crucial or a major factor[s]" to their vote.

Centrist and center-right Democrats increased their influence in the Democratic caucus, driven by unexpected gains in the South, which has a more right-leaning electoral base comparably than most of the country.

Nearly all Republican efforts to gain new seats through mid-decade redistricting failed to produce their intended effects, with North Carolina in particular unintentionally producing a Democratic majority in the state's congressional delegation.
However, progressives on the center-left also won due to the size of the wave election.
Over 30 pastors ran as Democrats in the 2026 election, and Reuters said that many of its candidates took socially conservative positions.
Axios reported an "epic power struggle" between the party's elected representatives on which policies to champion.

Time magazine reported that supporters of continued AI development "couldn't have had a worse night" and NBC News said that "Voters across the country delivered a sweeping rebuke to data center development in Tuesday’s midterm elections".
Voters approved over 40 measures to slow or ban data center growth over "concerns about public health, electricity prices, and environmental pollution."
Candidates "who tapped into voter fears won big" by supporting a superintelligence ban.
"Voters have had enough: they want strong and effective guardrails now, and they’re demanding accountability," Michael Kleinman, head of US policy for the Future of Life Institute, said.
"The AI reckoning is here."
In his victory speech, Senator Jon Ossoff warned that “the titans of Silicon Valley dig bunkers for themselves and warn that the artificial intelligence they’re creating risks human extinction.”
Abdul El-Sayed, the newly elected Michigan Senator, called for a “full-on pause” on frontier AI and also warned of human extinction.

Congresswoman Yassamin Ansari said that "Top of the Democratic agenda on day 1 needs to be a pause on advanced AI development, regulation of this out of control industry, and a ban on artificial superintelligence."
On Truth Social, President Trump said: "I wasn't on the Ballot and if I was, we would have won IN A LANDSLIDE!"
He repeated this to CBS News, where he also congratulated the Democrats, saying: "congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country."
Donald Trump acknowledged after the midterm elections that the war in Iran was a factor in the Republican loss.
He told Fox News that he would veto any "insane" bills the Democrats attempted to pass, adding, "And after a few months of vetoing them, they call and say, 'How do we do this?'
And we'll work together."
Some White House officials and Republican allies also called the war a mistake and said that if the conflict had ended sooner, the results of the midterm elections could have been different.
Vice President JD Vance blamed foreign policy for the results, saying "The real reason we lost is obvious to almost everyone … The reason we lost is the war.
The president himself said so last night" and added "If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so.
Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay.
Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest".
Vance said that voters want to 'change our relationship to Israel'.

Robert Garcia, who is set to chair the House Oversight Committee, issued a statement on November 3, after the Republican defeat in the elections, telling the Republicans to "lawyer up", a statement that showed the House Democrats' readiness to confront the Trump administration.

Garcia had previously said that in the event of a Democratic victory, he would conduct investigations into Elon Musk's role in the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), the Trump family's business activities, abuses by US Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE), and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal.

Former President Barack Obama said that the election's results showed that the American people want "a politics that brings people together rather than divides them" and leaders offering concrete solutions to their problems.
Along with the Republican election defeat in the US, Tesla shares fell by about 5%, and SpaceX shares fell by 6.9% in pre-market trading.

The Australian far-right political party One Nation distanced itself from Trump following the election, removing or editing pages that had referenced Trump or compared its platform to the Trump administration's policies.
Canada's minister responsible for Canada-U.S. Trade Dominic LeBlanc said that the election's results were interesting but would not change Canada's trade stance toward the United States.
Ontario's Premier Doug Ford struck a much more excited tone, joking about doing "cartwheels" as he watched results roll in, while stating the "cheese has slipped off the cracker" with Trump.
Nonetheless, Ford also stated he was under no illusions about the trade war being over.
France's minister for Europe and Foreign Affairs Jean-Noël Barrot declared that the election's results were "excellent news for American democracy".
German Chancellor Friedrich Merz commented that Trump had governed without involving Congress through executive orders and would probably continue to do so.
He believed that not much would change except the budget, which the Democrats would now be able to block from passing.

Iranian supreme leader Mojtaba Khamenei told Fars News Agency that "If there are still those who harbor even the slightest hope for a change in behavior or shifts in partisan and factional alignments within the oppressive system, or who believe that by offering concessions to America they can dissuade it from enmity toward the Iranian nation, they are gravely mistaken".

Iranian Parliament speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf wrote on X that "Conscience or the cost of living, Americans said NO TO WAR, and we endorse this message" and that "if the US govt betrays their public will to serve international paymasters and blackmailers, it will learn our NO comes with a Nightmare".

Supreme National Security Council secretary Mohsen Rezaei said on X that "The Iranian nation handed Trump a strategic defeat on the battlefield and in the Hormuz—and a POLITICAL DEFEAT in Washington" and that "Meanwhile, Americans got stuck with the bill for his war".

Norwegian prime minister Jonas Gahr Støre said that the election represented a "change of course among American voters", and that "voices [were] now emerging in American politics that are closer to us than the president and the administration have stood for, for example on climate and environment, and in foreign policy and development aid policy."

Spain's prime minister Pedro Sánchez responded to the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections, saying that American voters had rejected policies that impoverish people—along with hatred, sexism, climate denial, and the privileges of the elites.

In reacting to the results of the midterms, British Prime Minister Andy Burnham told BBC News that "I feel the world has an opportunity now to unite around the issue that is affecting us all, and that's the cost of living".
